uncited: Zoom-out Adaptation is a post-training optimization technique that adapts a pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model to render anti-aliased images at lower resolutions (zoom-out).
It solves the problem of geometric dilation and aliasing artifacts (e.g., thick spokes on wheels) that occur when a high-resolution model is viewed at a distance or downsampled.
**Inputs:** A pre-trained 3DGS model (positions, covariances, opacities, colors) trained on full-resolution ($\times 1$) images; camera poses for the target scene.
**Outputs:** An adapted 3DGS model optimized for low-resolution rendering.

The 3DGS model retains the standard structure: a list of $N$ Gaussians, each defined by mean position $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^3$, covariance matrix $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$ (or quaternion/scale), opacity $\alpha \in [0,1]$, and spherical harmonics coefficients for color.
Let $I_{HR}$ be the rendered image at the original resolution.
**Pseudo-GT Generation:** Downsample the high-resolution renderings to create the pseudo-ground truth $I_{pseudo}$ for the target resolution.
*   **Pseudo-GT Quality:** The quality of guidance varies by dataset.
For the Blender dataset (isolated objects), supervision is intensive and high-quality.

A technique to adapt a pre-trained 3DGS model for high-resolution rendering (zoom-in) by using a super-resolution network (SwinIR) to generate high-resolution pseudo-GT from low-resolution training data.
Unlike zoom-out, which downsamples renderings, this method upscales supervision.
*   **Memory Complexity:** No significant additional memory overhead during rendering, as it reuses the standard 3DGS structure.
The method addresses the limitation of standard 3DGS, which is optimized for a specific resolution and suffers from aliasing when viewed at different scales.
